title: Perception and misperception of surface opacity
research_question: How does the visual system compute the opacity of surfaces, specifically, how does the covariation of intensity and 3D surface orientation modulate the perception of surface opacity/translucency?

participants.description: Naïve observers (n ≥ 10 in each experiment) participated. Specific Ns for experiments were 10, 11, 14, 14, 9, 10, 14, 14.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Rendered images of 3D surfaces (bloated 'snake', twisted 'ribbon', 'bump', 'torus') with varying luminance gradients and light fields. Luminance gradients were either generated by translucent objects illuminated from within/behind or opaque objects illuminated externally. Image contrast was varied multiplicatively. Some stimuli included black dot or grid textures, or specular reflections. Stereoscopic views were used for 3D shape perception.

measures.instrument: Paired comparison task: observers selected the surface that appeared more translucent in each pair.
Implicitly inferred from shape and material perception.

findings.antecedent: Relationship between luminance gradients and perceived 3D surface orientation
findings.mechanism: The visual system uses the covariation of intensity and surface orientation as a cue to opacity.
findings.quote: identical luminance gradients can appear either translucent or opaque depending on the relationship between luminance and perceived 3D surface orientation

findings.antecedent: Opaque surfaces embedded in diffuse light fields (eliminating covariation between surface orientation and intensity)
findings.mechanism: Lack of intensity-orientation covariation is interpreted as subsurface scattering.
findings.quote: illusory percepts of translucency can be induced by embedding opaque surfaces in diffuse light fields that eliminate the covariation between surface orientation and intensity

findings.antecedent: Transparent materials embedded in light fields (generating images where surface orientation and intensity covary)
findings.mechanism: Intensity-orientation covariation is interpreted as surface reflection (shading).
findings.quote: illusory percepts of opacity can be generated when transparent materials are embedded in a light field that generates images where surface orientation and intensity covary

findings.antecedent: 3D shape interpretation (translucent-appearing shapes like 'snake' and 'torus' vs. opaque-appearing shapes like 'ribbon' and 'bump')
findings.mechanism: Shapes appearing translucent are perceived to transmit light from behind/inside, while opaque-appearing shapes are perceived to reflect light from above.
findings.quote: The shapes that appear translucent appear to transmit light from a source located behind or inside the object, whereas the shapes that appear opaque appear to reflect light from above.

findings.mechanism: Shapes where intensity and surface orientation do not covary (snake, torus) appear more translucent than shapes where they do covary (ribbon, bump).
findings.quote: The snake and torus appear more translucent than the ribbon and bump.

findings.mechanism: The effect of shape on perceived translucency is statistically significant.

findings.quote: The 3D shape interpretation also influences the effect of image contrast on perceived translucency, producing a significant interaction between the main effects of shape and contrast [counterclockwise from Fig. 2 A, Top Left: F(1, 9) = 12, P < 0.01...

findings.quote: The 3D shape interpretation also influences the effect of image contrast on perceived translucency, producing a significant interaction between the main effects of shape and contrast [... F(1, 10) = 12, P < 0.01...

findings.quote: The 3D shape interpretation also influences the effect of image contrast on perceived translucency, producing a significant interaction between the main effects of shape and contrast [... F(1, 13) = 60, P << 0.01...

findings.quote: The 3D shape interpretation also influences the effect of image contrast on perceived translucency, producing a significant interaction between the main effects of shape and contrast [... F(1, 13) = 18, P << 0.01].

findings.mechanism: Low contrast is a cue to translucency for certain shapes.
findings.quote: Decreasing contrast increases perceived translucency for the bump surface, consistent with the view that low contrast is a cue to translucency (18-20).

findings.mechanism: The effect of contrast on perceived translucency is nonmonotonic for these shapes.
findings.quote: However, the torus, snake, and ribbon shapes appear most translucent for moderate contrast values.

findings.antecedent: Physically translucent surface (illuminated from behind) with 'cylinder' shape
findings.consequent: Perceived as opaque and frontally illuminated
findings.mechanism: The shape interpretation (cylinder) leads to a misperception of material and illumination source.
findings.quote: Note that the lower shape appears translucent whereas the upper shape is misperceived to be opaque and frontally illuminated.

findings.mechanism: 3D shape has a larger influence on perceived surface opacity than contrast.
findings.quote: the effect of 3D shape had a larger influence on perceived surface opacity than contrast (Fig. S5).

findings.mechanism: The large effects of 3D shape on perceived opacity generalize to stimuli with specular reflections.
findings.quote: We again observed large effects of 3D shape on perceived opacity and comparatively smaller effects of contrast. Our results therefore generalize to stimuli with or without specular reflections.

findings.antecedent: Inconsistencies between intensity and surface normals (e.g., depth map textures, ramp shading)
findings.mechanism: Illusory translucency from depth map textures and ramp shading also depends on the relationship between intensity and local surface orientation.
findings.quote: Images that exhibit stronger inconsistencies between intensity and surface normals appear more translucent (the left object in Fig. S4) than those that generate spurious correlations between intensity and surface normals (the sphere in Fig. S4).

findings.antecedent: Locally convex surface patches (in bumpy Lambertian surface under natural illumination)
findings.mechanism: Convexities are less subject to disruptions from cast shadows and interreflections, preserving the covariation cue.
findings.quote: intensity covaries with surface normals on locally convex surface patches where cast shadows and interreflections are less likely.

findings.antecedent: Diffuse light field (for bumpy Lambertian surface)
findings.mechanism: Diffuse illumination removes the systematic covariation between intensity and surface orientation.
findings.quote: this covariation is not observed in the same regions for the variants of the surface in Fig. S2 that appear translucent (i.e., that were either rendered as translucent or rendered as opaque in a diffuse light field).

findings.consequent: Perceived surface opacity/translucency (with variations in surface pigmentation)
findings.mechanism: The dramatic effect of 3D shape on perceived surface opacity/translucency generalizes to stimuli with surface pigmentation.
findings.quote: We therefore performed additional experiments using stimuli containing variations is surface pigmentation, and observed the same dramatic effect of 3D shape on perceived surface opacity/translucency (Fig. S7).

mechanisms: The visual system uses the covariation of intensity and 3D surface orientation as a cue to infer the opacity of surfaces: smooth covariation suggests surface reflection (shading), while smooth but independent variation suggests light-material interactions within the object (subsurface scattering).
The computation of opacity/translucency occurs at a level of representation where 3D shape of surfaces is made explicit.
The visual system successfully segments the contributions of texture from smooth gradients generated by shading or subsurface scattering.

tables.description: Plots the proportion of trials that each stimulus was chosen as appearing more translucent than the other surfaces, as a function of luminance contrast, for different 3D shapes and shape cues (motion/disparity).

Shows results of a paired comparison experiment judging translucency for physically translucent surfaces (snake vs. cylinder shapes, translucent vs. opaque materials) across varying intensity (contrast).

limitations: Orientation-intensity plots were derived using ground truth surface orientations and intensities, not direct measurements of perceived shape.
The study does not explain how 3D shape can be computed from static monocular images.
Initial experiments investigated only uniform albedo surfaces, making generalization to densely varying surface albedo unclear (though later addressed by additional experiments).

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Significance
          One of the most perplexing problems in vision science is to understand how the visual system computes the reflectance and transmittance properties of different materials despite variability in 3D shape and illumination. We show that 3D shape can play a decisive role in the perception of surface opacity and that gross misperceptions of surface opacity can arise for specific surface geometries and light fields. We argue that the perception of surface opacity depends on the relationship between intensity and 3D surface orientation and show that this relationship can play a decisive role in modulating the perception of surface opacity, independently of the true physical characteristics of materials.
